title: When I Last Visited My School
summary: A reflection on the memories and emotions associated with visiting my old school.
content:
# When I Last Visited My School

Schools are one of the few places that remain the same against the flow of time. Most of the schools I have ever visited are still the same – the buildings, the offices, the labs, the lavatories, the drinking water tap, the ground, and even the paints. Many adults visit their school on a regular basis to feel nostalgia and recollect old memories. A few months ago, I was invited by my school to give a presentation on Early Leadership Development. I felt extremely honored and excited to visit my school where I spent 14 years of my life. I have always been deeply attached to my school.
When I was heading towards my school, it was around 9:30 in the morning. As I was walking past the roads and the alleys – I began to realize that the shops we used to buy things from have been replaced by other new shops. It was a strange feeling for me. I remember, I would walk on those roads with tremendous self-confidence, but now I felt as if I was lost.
I reached my school at around 9:45, and there I first saw our beloved gatekeeper daai. His name is Raajkumar, I had taught him to play table tennis, and he had improved a lot too. I asked him whether he still plays table tennis, he said that ever since we left, he has never touched a racket. I don’t know why but my heart was shattered. I asked him if the principal was in his office, he said he was, and I headed towards the principal office.
My feet knew where the office was. As I took those familiar steps, I could not process what was in front of my eyes. For 14 years, I studied in a single-story building school that had blue steel roof. We could read “HULAS STEEL” imprinted on the roof if we looked up from our classroom. Suddenly, I was in front of a U-shaped 5-storey building. The ground area had become small. The hall where we competed, learned, and developed ourselves was destroyed. To be real, everything had changed except a few teachers who taught me were still there. I met them, talked to them about their lives and realized even their behavior had changed. A teacher who would slap me almost daily because I never did my homework assigned by me was saying tapai to me. I felt like an alien there.
After we finished the session, I met with my juniors, and they loaded me with tons of questions. They didn’t inquire anything about the topic I was speaking on rather they asked about me, though. I happily spent time with them. They were very happy that the school they study in was upgraded significantly – the labs, the canteen, the library (we only had a bookshelf in every class), everything had upgraded. After everything was done, I left.
The school I had in my memory has already been replaced by the new school’s appearance. It is the place which sculpted almost every part of me. The place where I got my best friends, learned majority of what I know till today, unlocked my strengths, and built my overall character – is simply blown from there like dust. 
I wish to never go there again.

title: The Commodification of Spirit: How Gurus Are Taking The Seat Where God Once Sat
summary: It is a critical essay that explains how spirituality is often disguised as religion, and how it can be a tool for manipulation and control.
content:
# The Commodification of The Spirit: How Gurus Are Taking the Seat Where God Once Sat 

For centuries or even millennia, religion acted as a central institution for system in human society. It anchored socio-moral values, ethics, and faith ensuring a systematic society. It also institutionalized the idea of God and established a set of rules that were believed to bring people closer to God (or the divine). However, many studies show that with the advancements in science, education, storage of verified knowledge, and information systems, the degree of religious faith among individuals and society has significantly declined. This suggests that religion and the idea of God were historically crucial to sustain societal structure, uniformity, and sustainability – like the legal system in the contemporary world. Nevertheless, with the passage of time, they have simply begun to lose their grip over people's mind and the society as a whole.

In recent times, the term "spirituality" has gained a huge popularity across the world, not merely in South Asia. Still, what is the meaning of spirituality at first? The answer is not singular, as everyone holds a subjective definition of it. This vagueness makes the question more worth asking.

Many key philosophers and psychologists suggest different definitions of spirituality. However, here, I would emphasize how people across the globe generally understand it these days. The Cambridge Dictionary shows, “spirituality is the quality that involves deep feelings and beliefs of a religious nature, rather than the physical parts of life."

This means that spirituality fundamentally focuses on the non-materialistic or inner aspects of life. It emphasizes on an individual's bond with the universe or their own "inner self". It encourages individuals to explore where they personally find meaning – unlike traditional religions which impose strict obligations, rites, and rituals to please God.

Before we draw any conclusions or make assumptions about spirituality, we must take some social and natural facts into accounts.

First, the credibility and relevance of traditional religion have largely collapsed in the past century (or are gradually collapsing) due to accessibility to education, information, and knowledge. The decline in the percentage of religious people in censuses in developed and some developing nations is arguably the most concrete evidence of it. The population of religiously unaffiliated people has risen from 1.6 billion people (23%) in 2010, to 1.9 billion (24%) in 2020.

Article content
[Src: https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/06/09/religiously-unaffiliated-population-change/]
Second, many people feel lonely making them seek validation, reassurance, and a sense of belonging. Both religion and spirituality provide the very psychological supplements to meet these needs.

Third, people naturally experience moments of aha, epiphanies, and awe – which are indeed genuine and deeply meaningful. Some genuine human feelings of awe and wonder were either punished or suppressed by rigid religious beliefs. They were often redirected to God (or to the divine) too. Following the fall of religion’s credibility, there are many people who feel lost in this transition period. Now, they have no place to worship, pray, or confess with complete faith which leaves them isolated. Religion had remained as a trusted institution to anchor their morality, ethics, behaviour, and emotions.

I personally find the modern idea of spirituality to be quite two-faced. The basic building blocks of both religion and spirituality are almost identical. As we know, spirituality claims to oppose dogmatic socio-communal order and obligations. But it has its own hierarchy of spiritual teachers (Gurus) – which could be understandable to some extent. Nonetheless, spirituality relies heavily on unfalsifiable claims. Spirituality has effectively turned into a profit-driven industry selling people back their own egos in sacred makeup.

Amidst all of this, the primary concern is that spirituality may simply be the economic rebirth of religion. Historically, religions served as vital drivers to the economy, redistributing wealth through institutionalized obligations (no matter how hypocritical). The modern spirituality industry operates on the exact same framework. It has commercialized a psychologically fundamental human need: the desire to belong.

People used to donate wealth to temples and churches; now, they pay for so-called "spiritual" workshops.
Even though spirituality projects an identity of open-accessibility, numerous commercial ideas hide beneath it. For instance, certifications based on rankings; pay higher – get more valuable certificate. Retreat pricing (neo-gurudakshina to the spiritual instructor) might be justifiable, but how can you ever justify the certification-based rankings which are determined by the amount you pay? It is similar to buying fake educational degree certificates. However, to prevent themselves from rational questions the Gurus simply compare you with a Musk Deer (Kastoori Mriga) and enlightenment or inner-peace to its own aroma. This way, they trap you inside a capsule of belief they create using such absurd, symbolic, and unscientific comparisons.

If a spirit or any kind of spiritual essence resides within every person, why is financial transaction required to get a direct access to it? Did Siddhartha Gautama have a Guru to gain enlightenment? Did Nanak? Did Osho? Did Mahaveer?

In this sense, spirituality replicates platforms like Spotify, Claude, Canva, etc. The common principle is offering a basic version to all the users but reserve the "authentic" experience for premium paying customers.
When we talk about spirituality, the word "spirit" also follows. Regarding this term, Carl Jung defined it as an autonomous, non-material psychological reality experienced as an active, dynamic force. He argued that it brings meaning, inspiration, and higher consciousness to the human mind. He perceived the spirit as a subjective psychological core rather than any kind of metaphysical entity. He also relates it to the psyche, the deep mental structures driving human behaviour. [Src: https://www.jungiananalysts.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Gitz-Johansen-T.-JAP-2020-65-4-653-671-1.pdf ]

On the contrary, the so-called "spiritual leaders" push an absurdly unfalsifiable and metaphysical definition of the spirit. Oftentimes, they rob some natural and scientifically explainable emotional states like awe, aha, and epiphanies. They repackage simple human experiences into out-of-reality stories and fictions merely for commercial gain and socio-political influence.

Spirituality has acknowledged that external deities and authoritarian religions are losing credibility. Which is why, it has shifted its focus from the external to the internal also known as "the inner self." It has basically relocated the office of faith-based influence from an external God to an "internalized spirit" or "cosmic self".
By convincing followers that the entire universe resides within them, spiritual leaders present standard human emotions as evidence of cosmic truth. In my personal opinion, this shift can be far more dangerous than traditional religions because of two reasons. First, human ego could possibly take a much darker form when individuals begin to view themselves as "divine" or "chosen ones". Second, the spiritual leaders (Gurus) take the seat previously occupied by traditional God.

Rejecting an external God is relatively easy because God is defined as a separate entity from us which can neither be seen, heard, nor felt. On the other hand, rejecting the idea of an internal spirit feels extremely similar to denying one's own existence and presence in the universe.

Blind obedience to external authority like God might often indicate lack of rationality and critical thinking in an individual. Nevertheless, believing that you have the whole universe within yourself or you are the avatar of the universe itself may pose immeasurably higher intellectual, moral, and social risks. Moreover, when someone holding such beliefs does a morally unjustifiable act, the belief itself becomes a justification or excuse – just like Krishna having multiple love affairs in the name of “leela” just because he’s God.  Hence, there is no external moral, social, and ethical standard left to call wrong as wrong.

I personally find no distinction between people believing in such unfalsifiable and egoistic ideas and Raskolnikov (from Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment) in his early days when he firmly believed that he was not an ordinary man and people like him were morally exceptional. Later, driven by this belief, Raskolnikov ends up committing two murders.

When traditional religious institutions lost their grip over the society's power dynamics, "the old guards" of religion subtly remoulded religion into spirituality to retain their influence. Some argue that spirituality as a different practice was into existence long before the decline of religions started – which is absolutely true.  However, my simple question to them is, "Why has it become popular at this phase of our civilization?" "Why was it not popular back then?" The answer is simple – religions were already powerful so, they did not need spirituality back then to indoctrinate people and sustain their socio-political dominance and finances.

Following the decline of religions, “the old guards” refurbished the concept of spirituality and made it fancy. The distinction from traditional religions that made spirituality more popular is that this new replica is more private and self-centred. This could be dangerous. Another difference is that it is far less accountable because questioning yourself is very complex and difficult than questioning an external God or religious faith. Now matter what, spirituality has already been successful in maintaining a good financial revenue and authority over public faith.

While practices like mindfulness, expression of gratitude, and meditation might help to promote self-awareness, connection with nature, and peace of mind, they need not be bought through financial transactions like retreat pricing or any kind of subscription. I personally do not understand how people are drawn to services like "body-count reset rituals," where the so-called Gurus reset the number of sexual partners you've had back to zero. Such services do not directly contribute to promoting self-awareness and mindfulness – they are just ways of looting people financially, emotionally, and psychologically.

People who believe in real spirituality practice meditation, gratitude, or a sense of connection to something they feel is beyond themselves – without any Guru. They neither purchase any product nor believe in any metaphysical claim about being divine. This “non-commercial spiritual” practice is at least better than the previously mentioned practices where people only spend their time, money, and energy unnecessarily.

However, the irony of spirituality hasn’t yet ended yet. What people think is spiritual is actually biological and psychological rather "spiritual". The wonderful experiences you have during or after meditating or expressing gratitude is an outcome of your mind releasing neurochemicals like serotonin, dopamine, oxytocin, etc. These neurochemicals make you happy and feel at peace – similar to listening to a music you love or being with your loved ones. And when people are unaware of this process occurring in their brains – human behaviour plays a role to justify or explain it anyhow to us. Consequently, people relate this neurochemical process to a connection with "the divine" or something beyond themselves because they do not understand what is happening inside their brain. This is exactly where the tale of Musk Deer is introduced by the Gurus.

So, practicing meditation and gratitude doesn't need to be contemplated essentially as “spiritual” – but it is a matter of personal choice though. Following this, I also believe that many institutes teaching yoga, meditation, gratitude, and mindfulness should stop calling themselves anything like “spiritual wellness/recovery centre”. They can simply promote mental well-being in its naked and scientific form without using any “sacred” or “spiritual” packaging. Living with thoughts based on empirical facts could be challenging to many people yet it is incomparable to believing in metaphysical, fictional, and unfalsifiable ideas and living by them.

Essentially, what spirituality sells us is merely psychological as well as philosophical to some extent. Therefore, the existence of this industry is even more irrelevant and less structured as compared to religions with far more dangers too.
In this way, modern-day spirituality has refurbished religion and robbed what is scientifically explainable for the sake of economic gain and socio-political influence. Still, if someone insists on walking in the spiritual route to validate their “inner self”, I firmly believe that they should at least remember that the “spiritual” claims and geocentric thoughts aren't much different in terms of evidence, logic, and rationality.

title: Meaning of the name - Prasham
summary: It is a narrative essay as a blog post that explains the story and the meaning of my name.
background: We were given an assignment at UNepal, where we were told to find out the meanings of our names. So, I decided to include it in my writings section as well.
content:
# Meaning of “Prasham”

I was named Prasham the day I was born – contrary to what mostly happens in Hindu families where they name a child on the 11th day of his/her birth. A neighbor of ours at the time, whom we call ‘Anu Didi,’ named me so. Her logic was pretty simple; she took the first syllables from my elder sister’s name (Pragya), father’s name (Shyam), and mother’s name (Manju). In this way, I became Prasham.

I was unaware of my name’s meaning until I was ~14. For that reason, I disliked it as well. To me, it sounded very feminine as I had always (and still do) admired names such as: Dalabhanjan, Chandraprakash, Shatrumardan, Rudrapratap, and so on as they sound very intimidating, hefty, and macho.

Whenever someone asked me about the meaning of my name, for a very long period of my life, I had no answers to give them. So, I just had to say “I don’t know.” Or “This word doesn’t exist anywhere else.” I can’t remember how many times I’ve blamed Anu Didi for giving me a name that was empty on the outside, yet felt heavy to have. Some relatives also disdained my name by calling it a foreign-culture-influenced name. A few of them even confronted my mother about it right in front of me when I was still a child. Despite experiencing those incidents, I myself have never liked parents giving their children imported names from the English novels and stories (for e.g., Richmond, James, Jessica) – and I still don’t. So, no hard feelings towards them.

However, when I Googled “प्रशम” – the search engine took me to Wiktionary (विकिशब्दकोश). When I opened the webpage, I discovered that the word was composed as: 
प्र + शम = प्रशम [Src: sa.wiktionary.org/wiki/प्रशम] Where:
- प्र = A prefix (उपसर्ग) which means: intense, complete; special; and forward/upward. 
[Src: प्रज्ञा नेपाली बृहत् शब्दकोश]
- शम = A state of mental peace; to cultivate inner peace; self-control over senses/impulses; a feeling of peacefulness; to forgive; to neutralize chaos. [Src: प्रज्ञा नेपाली बृहत् शब्दकोश]

When I personally analyzed how the prefix Pra- is used in various terms in the Amarkosh and Nepali Shabdakosh, I got to the conclusion that in case of my name, it best means “complete” or “intense”.
Therefore, the closest meaning of my name could possibly be – an intense feeling of stable peacefulness through restrained senses. It can also be interpreted as to completely neutralize something. I hope to own its meaning too.

I’ve searched the entire internet yet found no other Prasham. Now, I feel quite glad that I have this unique name and I love it – now, I wish I could even patent it. All thanks to Anu Didi and my family who decided to keep it.

title: Is All Technology in the Vedas?
summary: Genuine respect for ancient thinkers means allowing their ideas to be studied honestly. Turning every myth, metaphor, and miracle into a claim about modern technology is not how we should study the past. Stop retrospectively attributing modern discoveries to ancient texts and calling it Vedic glory.
background: This is an essay I wrote during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
content:
# Is All Technology In The Vedas?
*How Mythology, Politics, And Post-Truth Thinking Distort Science & History*



The slogan “All modern technology is already in the Vedas” sounds impressive at first. It gives us a nice feeling that our ancestors were smarter than we are. They knew everything before the west even existed. In contemporary India, claims about ancient scientific achievements have also appeared in political rhetoric and public discourse. They are seen using it to sell national pride wrapped in religious scripture. Similar trend has started to be seen in Nepal as well.

But once you put this claim next to history, archaeology, and basic scientific logic, it collapses. It is not just wrong. It is intellectually dishonest too.

This article explains why the “Vedas have all technology” story is a myth, and why treating religious texts as scientific manuals is a mistake with real consequences.

Stop Stealing Credit from Real Science

Some people who repeat this claim either do not understand science or do not simply care. They ignore a basic distinction. It is useful to distinguish scientific discovery from technological invention. Discovering a natural phenomenon is different from innovating a reproducible technology. 

Modern technology is not a gift from the gods. It is the result of long, hard, systematic work. Research, experiments, failures, corrections, peer review are the pillars of it. It takes place in labs, workshops, and universities. Not in hymns and rituals.

Saying “it was already in the Vedas” is a cheap way to steal credit from real scientists and replace methodology with mythology. If you want the credit for science, please show the labs, the data, and concrete results. Not a verse that can be twisted to mean anything after the fact.



The Vedas Are Oral and Ritual Texts, Not Engineering Blueprints

The Vedic collections were transmitted through highly developed oral traditions for centuries. The surviving manuscript record is much later than the period in which the texts were originally composed. 

What are the Vedas, fundamentally? The simple answer: hymns to deities, ritual instructions (stotras, mantras), and cosmological as well as philosophical reflections.

Do they contain any among: diagrams (or technical drawings), mathematical formulas for engineering, guided experiments (or error-correction mechanisms), practical procedures for building complex machines?

It is because the Vedas do not function as engineering manuals containing reproducible technical designs for sophisticated machines. They are fundamentally ritual texts.

Archaeological evidence from ancient India (including the Indus Valley) does show Bronze Age technology. For e.g., stone, copper, and bronze tools; advanced urban planning. But this evidence does not demonstrate the advanced machines, electrical systems, or technical blueprints claimed by modern Vedic-technology narratives.

Some even suggest that vitrified (glassy) bricks found at sites like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the result of some kind of nuclear explosion. They further add that the nuclear explosion had taken place during the time of The Mahabharata war. They claim the nuclear explosion to be caused by Brahmastra used in the Mahabharata war. Some modern writers interpret the Brahmastra as a weapon capable of causing long-term environmental damage.

However, the nuclear interpretation requires archaeological, geological, and radiometric evidence that has not been demonstrated. Vitrified material alone is not evidence of a nuclear explosion. Therefore, vitrified bricks are not proof of the existence of nuclear technology in ancient Indian subcontinent. Consequently, a destructive supernatural weapon in an epic narrative cannot be the evidence of nuclear technology.

Viman Shastra: A Modern, Debunked Text

The Vaimanika Shastra, (often called the Viman Shastra) is frequently used as “proof” that ancient India had aircraft. But in reality, it is one of the weakest links in this entire narrative.

•	The surviving Vaimanika Shastra manuscript is associated with Pandit Subbaraya Shastry and dates to the early twentieth-century manuscript tradition. Its attribution to the ancient sage Bharadvaja is not supported by evidence establishing an ancient date. Even Yuval Noah Harari’s essay – ‘Humility’ is wrong about the author of Vaimanika Shastra where he mentions it to be composed by Sage Bharadwaj.

•	In 1974, a team of 5 aeronautical and mechanical engineers from the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru including H.S. Mukunda, S.M. Deshpande, H.R. Nagendra, S.P. Govindaraju, and A. Prabhu studied the aircraft described in the text. They concluded that the designs were aeronautically unfeasible and called them “a decided impossibility.”



The geometry of the aircraft describes was found to be completely unsuitable for flight. The propulsion (thrust) ideas would resist flying rather than enable it. 



This is not a minor issue. A text does not become scientific just because it uses words like “engine,” “fuel,” or “aircraft.” Technical vocabulary is not technical knowledge. A real technical document must provide designs that obey physical laws and can be built, tested, and reproduced. The Viman Shastra fails that test.



Some people advocate modern spacecraft like SpaceX’s Dragon Capsule, NASA Orion, and the historically renowned Apollo capsules resemble Rukma Viman (an aircraft mentioned in Vimanika Shastra). It turns out that the Rukma Viman was unfeasible for flight. Those modern spacecrafts were designed with a conical base to push intense frictional heat away from the capsule while landing. It also kept the spacecraft balanced as it fell through the atmosphere.

Henceforth, claiming that NASA and SpaceX replicated the designs from Vaimanika Shastra cannot be considered as an act of wisdom or fairness.



A Political Example: Pushpak Viman

This mix-up between myth and technology still shows up in politics. In June 2026, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath spoke about Ayodhya’s new air connectivity and referred to Lord Rama arriving in the mythical Pushpak Viman. He contrasted the ancient account of Pushpak Viman with the long gap before modern air services returned to Ayodhya.

A remark like this can be read as mythology, symbolism, or political theatre. But bring it up as part of the history of aviation, and it becomes misleading. A flying chariot in the Ramayana is not evidence of an engineered aircraft. If it were, we'd need actual blueprints, physical parts left behind by whoever built it, and a real tradition of flight passed down—not just a story from an epic.

A mythological vehicle and an aircraft are not the same thing. One comes from religious imagination and literature. The other needs an engine that produces real thrust, materials that can survive flight stress, and years of testing before anything actually leaves the ground.



Sushruta Samhita: Great Science, but Not “Vedic Science”

The Sushruta Samhita is undoubtedly a genuine historical achievement. It contains detailed discussions of surgery, anatomy, wounds, and the instruments Sushruta's tradition used to treat them. Sushruta deserves recognition for the medical knowledge associated with his tradition.

But this achievement should not be used to prove that his scientific ideas existed in the Vedas. The Sushruta Samhita belongs to the Ayurvedic medical tradition, often described as an Upaveda – a separate body of knowledge. It is not one of the four Vedas or the 18 Puranas. For e.g., there is another Upaveda called Dhanurved (an ancient science of archery and military warfare). Will it be wise to credit the ideas of Dhanurved – a non-religious book to Vedas which are religious texts by category?

That distinction matters because Sushruta was indeed a genius. When an ancient Indian physician made a contribution to surgery, the appropriate response is to study and credit that medical tradition directly. Modern medical-history does recognize the importance of Sushruta Samhita. It is unnecessary to attach the achievement to the Vedas in order to make them appear more prestigious or superior to other religious scriptures.

Calling Sushruta’s work “Vedic science” is therefore a form of retrospective branding. We should call Sushruta what the historical evidence supports. For e.g., a physician, surgeon, and medical writer. Imagine the Italians labeling daVinci’s writings as a part of Roman Catholic legacy. If it sounds unfair, then how can associating Sushruat’s work with the Vedas be fair? 

Furthermore, the Prime Minister of India Mr. Narendra Modi made a similar kind of claim in 2014 while speaking at the inauguration of a hospital in Mumbai. He suggested that the story of Ganesha’s elephant head indicate the existence of an ancient plastic surgeon in the ancient India. And, he also mentioned that the story of Karna’s birth hinted towards the knowledge of genetic science.

These stories may be used as cultural or theological narratives, but they do not constitute scientific evidence for reconstructive surgery or genetics. A mythological story about an elephant-headed deity is not evidence of reconstructive surgery. Similarly, a miraculous birth story is not evidence of genetics, embryology, or stem-cell technology. Real surgery and real genetics require anatomy, instruments, biological mechanisms, experimental evidence, and reproducible procedures. None of these are described in the Vedas or the Puranas. Plus, it would be unscientific to believe that those could happen with the power of consciousness, manifestation, or any kind of metaphysical devices.

Hence, it will be wise to say that a myth resembles a modern idea instead of saying that an ancient society possessed the relevant science or technology. Similarity of imagery is not proof of historical knowledge.



Retrofitting: Post-Truth Propaganda

A clear pattern emerges whenever these claims are examined.

First, a modern discovery or invention becomes known. Then, someone searches ancient scriptures, epics, or commentaries for words that can be interpreted as referring to it. Once a vague and symbolic resemblance is found, the resemblance is presented as proof that the modern discovery had already been known thousands of years ago.

This is not prediction that the ancient people made. It is retrospective reinterpretation done by the modern society themselves.

A genuine prediction would require a text to provide a clear, specific, understandable, and technically meaningful description before the discovery was made. It should identify the relevant mechanism, make a testable claim, and allow independent readers to understand what is being predicted without the aid of modern afterthought.

A vague reference to a flying vehicle is not a description of an aircraft. A divine weapon is not a nuclear bomb. A miraculous birth is not genetic engineering. A cosmic metaphor is not a theory of relativity.

The standard is often changed after the fact. When a verse happens to resemble a modern concept, it is called scientific foresight. When countless other verses do not match reality, they are ignored. In psychology, this is known as confirmation bias. You accept the apparent matches while silently discarding the mismatches. Some prominent Indian scientists have explicitly rejected this approach.

•	Meghnad Saha wrote that after decades of searching the Vedas, Upanishads, Puranas, and Shastras, he found no root of modern science in them.

•	J.V. Narlikar said claims that “all modern discoveries of science are of Vedic origin” do not stand up to scientific inspection. He warned that a “past glory mentality” was dangerous for India’s future because it stifled progress, misunderstood science, and harmed the texts themselves.

This is not ancient wisdom. It is modern insecurity dressed up as tradition. Nations with Hindu-majority populations like India and Nepal should insist on looking forward. They must have a modern scientific temper instead of looking backward for imaginary and so-called ancient technologies.



Zero Archaeological Evidence

If ancient India truly had flying machines, time-travel devices, nuclear weapons or energy plants, and advanced industrial technology, we should have found at least one of the workshops, factories, and production sites.

Where are the tools, engines, and instruments? Where is the consistent iconography of real machines (not the symbolic chariots)? Where are the technical treatises with reproducible instructions?

Mainstream archaeologists and scholars find no credible evidence of technology beyond the Bronze Age tool set in the Indus Valley or later Vedic contexts. No factories. No engines. No instruments. No patents. This means, zero evidence to rely upon.

That is mythology, not engineering, and we must accept this fact with an open mind. We should move forward leaving the past glory mindset aside. Nevertheless, we should keep in mind that some traditions, rituals, festivals and so on are our cultural assets. We must not discard them in the name of scientific progress.



Methodological Gap: No Scientific Method in Scripture

Even a Grade-10 student is aware of the basic outline of scientific inquiry: observation, hypothesis, experiment, replication, peer review, and criticism as well.

Scientific claims always remain open to testing and correction. A theory may be revised or rejected when evidence contradicts it. That capacity for self-correction is one of science’s greatest strengths and beauty.

In contrast, religious scriptures operate through a different kind of authority:

•	Revelation or sacred tradition

•	Authority of the text

•	Commentary and interpretation

•	Resistance to falsification

A claim about the physical world that cannot even be principally be tested or shown to be wrong is not functioning as a scientific hypothesis. It is an unfalsifiable claim. A system that can be never proven wrong is not science. It is dogma. Here, every line can be explained as prediction or Vedic foresight through metaphor, symbolism, mistranslation, or hidden meaning. In this way, baseless claims are protected from testing and counterarguments rather than supported by evidence.

Claims that “quantum uncertainty is in Vedanta” or “relativity is in the Bhagavad Gita” do absolute injustice to both science and religious philosophy. They shrink complex scientific theories to symbolic word associations, and turn religious scriptures into containers for whatever modern concept someone wants to find in them.



Why This Myth Is Pushed?

The “all technology is in the Vedas” narrative is not merely an innocent misunderstanding. It serves several political and ideological purposes even if it is unintentional:

I.	It can produce nationalist pride, “Our ancestors already knew everything.”

II.	It can reinforce religious authority, “The scripture is the ultimate source of knowledge.”

III.	It can also support an anti-modern narrative, “Modern science is foreign, while ancient scripture was already superior.”

The problem is not pride in historical achievements. Ancient South Asian scholars made important contributions in literature, philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and so on. However, the problem begins when genuine achievements are exaggerated into preposterous claims and later attributed to texts that do not contain them at the first place.

Some political and religious commentators exploit this confusion because it is emotionally effective. Public figures lacking even basic training in physics, engineering, archaeology, history of science, or textual criticism should especially be evaluated regardless of their beliefs and political status. Some of them speak with great certainty about aircraft, genetics, nuclear weapons, quantum physics, and relativity to provoke the public emotions into their favour.

For example, BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi has used the names of prominent scientists to suggest that modern science has deep Vedic origins. He has referred to Julius Robert Oppenheimer and the Bhagavad Gita, Niels Bohr and the Upanishads, and Hermann Oberth and the Vedas.

But these strongly willed associations do not verify what he claims. Oppenheimer’s proximity with the Bhagavad Gita does not mean that the Gita contained knowledge of nuclear physics. A scientist’s interest in a philosophical or religious text does not prove that the text had already predicted his/her scientific finding. Inspiration, personal admiration, or cultural influence is not the same as technical knowledge.

Arguments like “A scientist read (or took inspiration from) a Hindu text. Therefore, the scientific theory or invention is the outcome of the description contained in that text.” are completely irrelevant.

Politicians and influencers may use the prestige of science without accepting the discipline of science. They cite renowned scientists, isolated quotations, and vague similarities, but avoid the things that would actually matter as follows:

•	Precise textual evidence

•	Reliable dating of the passage

•	A clear translation

•	A technically accurate description

•	Material or archaeological corroboration

•	Independent testing and reproducibility

People should therefore be extremely cautious when public figures make such kinds of extraordinary claims about ancient science. The issue is not whether they hold religious beliefs. The issue is whether they are presenting mythology as history and symbolism as engineering.

When politicians use religion to claim scientific superiority, citizens should ask what evidence supports the claim and who benefits from its circulation. Such persuasive devices can generate applause, votes, and online engagement, but it does not produce knowledge nor promote growth.

It also discourages scientific education. If people are told that all knowledge was already present in scripture, they may begin to regard laboratories, universities, experiments, and critical research as unnecessary. That is not civilizational confidence. It is intellectual stagnation disguised as pride.



Misinterpretation of Poetry as Patents

Ancient thinkers had imagination. So do children, science-fiction writers, and novelists. We should regard imagination without evidence as myth-making rather than discovery. Innovation is something else entirely in this scenario.

I acknowledge the fact that imagination, creativity and curiosity are the valuable seeds of all the innovation. The Vedas are full of both real and fake seeds; science is the forest that actually flourished. F or that reason, claiming scientific accomplishments as a hidden achievement of the Vedas merely because a verse can be interpreted to resemble a modern discovery does not honor ancient knowledge; it distorts it. 

We must respect the creativity of ancient poets and philosophers. Yet calling their imaginary visions “technology” just because you can stretch a verse to sound like a modern invention and claim scientific credit is not just.

Ancient Indian sub-continental civilization does not need fictional achievements to deserve historical recognition. Indian mathematicians, astronomers, physicians, grammarians, philosophers and engineers made genuine contributions which can be studied through real historical evidence. The achievements of Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara, Panini, Sushruta and others are impressive precisely because they can be investigated as historical intellectual achievements. Turning every mythological image into a modern technological claim does not strengthen this legacy; it obscures it.



Conclusion: Stop Calling Myths “Vedic Glory”

Claiming that “all technology is in the Vedas” is not a demonstration of knowledge; it is an exercise in retrospective hijacking. The Vedas are ancient religious texts concerned with hymns, rituals, deities, cosmology, and sacred tradition. They are not engineering manuals containing the hidden blueprints of modern civilization.

The Vaimanika Shastra, often presented as evidence of ancient aviation, is a modern text whose aircraft designs failed simple scientific examination. The Sushruta Samhita represents a valuable medical tradition. However, it is not a Veda or Purana. Sushruta’s achievements should be studied and credited as medical history rather than being attached to scripture for political or religious prestige.

The same pattern appears when politicians connect Ganesha’s elephant head with plastic surgery, Karna’s birth with genetic science, or Pushpak Viman with aviation. These claims confuse mythological imagery with technical knowledge. They are not supported by the scientific method, textual criticism, or archaeological evidence.

Modern science was not created by stretching ancient verses until they resemble contemporary discoveries. It emerged through observation, experiment, mathematics, engineering, criticism, and repeated testing.

If ancient India actually had airplanes, nuclear technology, advanced genetics, or industrial machinery, then the evidence should be available like: factories, tools, engines, materials, technical drawings, manufacturing systems, and reproducible designs. Until such evidence is discovered, these claims merely remain mythology falsely presented as history.

The problem isn't believing that ancient Indians were intelligent. The problem is claiming ancient technological knowledge without evidence.

People should be skeptical especially when politicians and influencers make these claims without any expertise in the relevant fields. Religion can be used to create emotional loyalty, national pride, and political obedience. But again, none of those things can substitute for evidence.

Respecting the past does not mean inventing (or remoulding) a past. Genuine patriotism does not require falsehood. And genuine respect for ancient thinkers means allowing their ideas to be studied honestly. Turning every myth, metaphor, and miracle into a claim about modern technology is not how we should study the past.

Stop retrospectively attributing modern discoveries to ancient texts and calling it “Vedic glory.”ss

title: Why Philosophy over Self-help Culture
summary: It is a critical essay that compares philosophy and self-help culture.
background: This is the an essay I wrote during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
content:
# Why Philosophy Over Self-Help Culture?

It has become fashionable to read self-help books, listen to motivational speeches, and post inspirational quotations on social media. Ironically, these activities are often associated with personal growth, even when they produce little lasting change. On the contrary, reading serious literature or philosophical works is sometimes viewed as performative. For instance, a person seen reading Nietzsche's 'Beyond Good and Evil' may be perceived as a pseudo-intellectual, while someone carrying a popular self-help book is more likely to be praised for trying to improve. This change reflects a broader shift in how people understand self-improvement and life as a whole. Rather than examining difficult questions about truth, suffering, morality, and the purpose of life, many people now prefer books that promise momentary confidence, productivity, and success. Self-help culture is attractive because it offers comfort and simple solutions, but philosophy is ultimately more valuable because it does not merely reassure people that they are already complete; it challenges them to examine their weaknesses, question their goals, and take responsibility for the person they become.

The rise in the popularity of self-help culture is completely understandable. Many people experience anxiety, confusion, loneliness, failure, and uncertainty – which is rising day by day, yet they don't know how to respond to these experiences. Self-help books offer accessible advice in the form of routines, exercises, strategies, affirmations, and motivational messages. They may suggest readers to wake up early, set goals, develop positive habits, improve their confidence, or change their mindset. Such advice can be useful. A person who is disorganized in his life may benefit from learning how to manage time, while someone struggling with a bad habit may need a practical method to begin changing. Self-help is attractive because it transforms complicated problems into simple instructions. It gives readers the feeling that improvement is within reach.

However, the accessibility of self-help has eventually become its weakness as well. Many self-help books reduce complex human issues to formulas and slogans. They may propose that success depends mainly on a person’s attitude, discipline, or ability to think positively. This approach to thinking makes life appear more controllable than it really is. Human beings are affected not only by their choices but also by various factors like illness, poverty, social expectations, family circumstances, injustice, and several other random events. A simple, generic, and superficial promise that “anyone can achieve anything” may sound inspiring, but it doesn't adequately represent the constraints of real life. Instead of helping people understand their circumstances, it may lead them to blame themselves whenever they fail and vice versa if, in case, they succeed.

As a person who's vehemently passionate in philosophy and psychology, I've observed that self-help culture also depends heavily on emotional validation and temporary motivation. Many books tell readers that they are already good enough, that they deserve success, and that they should believe in themselves. Such encouragement can be helpful, especially for people who are overwhelmed by shame, guilt, and insecurity. Nevertheless, feeling encouraged is not the same as becoming disciplined, wise, or morally better. The excitement created by a motivational speech or an inspirational book often fades after a short time. Once the emotional energy disappears, the reader may return to the same habits and problems as before.

Therefore, motivation isn't an absolute form of change. It may help a person begin, but it cannot always explain the inevitability of change or how it should be sustained. A person might feel inspired to become more productive, but productivity by itself does not create a meaningful life. Someone may set ambitious goals and achieve them, yet remain dissatisfied because the goals were based on social pressure rather than personal conviction or will. Without a more profound understanding of one's purpose, self-improvement can become an endlessly absurd cycle. The individual constantly searches for another habit to build, another weakness to correct, and another goal to achieve, but never feels content within.

This is where philosophy offers a more rigorous alternative. Philosophy does not simply ask how people can become more successful or comfortable. It asks what success, comfort, happiness, freedom, and wellness actually mean. It confronts naked truths that motivational culture often avoids, like human beings are mortal, suffering is unavoidable, failure can't be eliminated, and countless aspects of life are far beyond our control. These truths can be harsh, but they can also make people more mature. A person who understands that life cannot be controlled entirely may become less reliant on false promises and affirmations. A person who accepts the inevitability of death may think more seriously about how to use their limited time.

Philosophy also challenges people to examine their weaknesses instead of covering them under positive sentences. Self-acceptance is indeed valuable, but we should not confuse it with self-satisfaction. A person may possess some inborn worth and still be dishonest, selfish, lazy, ignorant, or undisciplined. Being worthy of dignity does not mean being free from the responsibility to improve. Philosophy encourages people to confront the distinction between the person they imagine themselves to be and the person their actions reveal.

This demanding attitude can be found in the philosophical tradition of the examined life. To examine one’s life is to question one’s beliefs, desires, and habits rather than accepting them automatically and believing that you're sufficient. Philosophy asks individuals to consider whether they are pursuing goals because they truly value them or because society has indoctrinated them to do so. It asks whether money, status, fame, and even productivity are genuinely valuable or whether they have become superficial substitutes for happiness and meaning. Self-help may teach a person how to achieve a goal, but philosophy asks whether that goal actually deserves the person’s time and effort in the first place.

For example, a self-help book may teach someone how to work more efficiently to gain a promotion. Philosophy may ask whether the promotion is worth sacrificing health, friendship, family, or moral integrity. A self-help book may encourage someone to become more confident. Philosophy may ask whether confidence is based on self-awareness and strong self-esteem or merely on the desire to appear successful in front of society. A self-help book may encourage constant self-improvement; philosophy asks whether the will to improve comes from genuine inner knowledge or from the belief that one is never good enough according to people.

Nevertheless, philosophy also has its limitations too. Philosophical works can be difficult, vague, abstract, and disconnected from immediate practical problems. A person struggling with procrastination may need a concrete strategy rather than a discussion of human nature. Reflection without real action can become just another form of avoidance. Therefore, it would be unfair to claim that self-help has zero value. Practical advice can help people develop habits, recover from failure, and begin taking responsibility for their choices.

The better argument is that self-help should be treated as a tool rather than a complete perspective. Self-help materials may provide techniques, but philosophy provides direction. Self-help can teach people how to move forward, while philosophy helps them decide where and why they should go. In this sense, self-help is like a collection of tools, whereas philosophy is a compass. Tools are useful, but they cannot determine whether a person is actually building something meaningful. A person can become more efficient at pursuing goals that are empty, unhealthy, or imposed by others.

Rest must also be understood carefully. Rest is not necessarily a sign of weakness, and people sometimes need it to recover from exhaustion or illness. The problem occurs when comfort and a fake sense of self-satisfaction become permanent excuses for avoiding responsibility. Philosophy doesn't demand endless productivity, but it does demand honesty, integrity, and commitment to one's principles. It asks whether a person is resting because rest is genuinely necessary or because difficult work and self-examination are being avoided. Acceptance should rebuild a person for meaningful action, not permanently replace action.

Ultimately, self-help books are attractive because they promise that personal transformation can be achieved through simple methods and positive beliefs. They offer comfort at a time when many people feel uncertain, and they can provide useful motivation. Yet, their encouragement often fades when it is not supported by a more profound understanding of life. Philosophy offers something more difficult but more lifelong. It does not merely tell people that they are already enough; it asks them to become more truthful, responsible, thoughtful, and courageous. Self-help may teach people how to improve themselves, but philosophy asks the more important question: what kind of person should they become, and what kind of life is worth pursuing?

title: Testimonial featured in the book 'The Power of Mindset' by Dr. Rajendra KC
summary: Read it if you want to know what I think about the book 'The Power of Mindset' by Dr. Rajendra KC.
background: This is the testimonial I wrote for the book 'The Power of Mindset' by Dr. Rajendra KC, which was published in the book.
dedication: To all the readers of this book.
content:
# Validating, Inspiring, and Calling for Grounded Action 

“THE POWER OF MINDSET” stands out as a timely, bold, and critically important work that diagnoses Nepal’s education challenges with both clarity and empathy, while offering forward-looking ideas for students, parents, and educators alike. Its conversational and motivational tone, inclusive stakeholder perspective, and emphasis on mental health, applied learning, and collaboration make it both engaging and relevant. As a Gen Z reader, I find the book deeply validating - I can see my own experiences reflected in its critiques - and it also inspires me to think differently about learning and growth. However, some solutions lean toward idealism and could be better grounded in Nepal’s structural realities, such as rural infrastructure gaps, policy limitations, and economic constraints. The reliance on international examples may also feel distant for students outside urban or private-school contexts, highlighting the need for more local, relatable cases and tiered solutions that address both elite and public-school settings. Overall, it is a strong and motivational foundation - sharp in diagnosis and inspiring in vision - yet it would benefit from deeper contextual grounding and practical adaptability. The author’s personal journey remains one of the most powerful and motivating elements, reinforcing the book’s core message for Nepali youth.

title: मुक्तकहरू
summary: This is the collection of all the muktaks I've written till now. It is a forever work-in-progress section, and will be updated regularly.
background: This is the collection of all the muktaks written by me.
content:
# मुक्तक सङ्ग्रह

याद आयो अचनक आफैँले च्यातेको त्यो चिठी,
कति बिस्तारै लेखेको थिए त्यो नयाँ कागजमा चिठी।
चिठीको चिता त फोहोर उठेउनेले कहाँ लागिसके,
तर  बेलाबेला भूत बानी तर्साउन आउँछ अझै चिठी।

माग्दै नमागेको जीवनको छ ऋण थुप्रो तिर्नुपरेको,
बाध्यताले नै हो मैले पनि यहाँ जीवन बाँच्नुपरेको,
एकैछिन खुसी हुदाँ कस्तो हुन्थ्यो होला खै,
भारी मन लुकाउन छ मन्द मुस्कानले छोप्नुपरेको।

बाटोमा फुलिरहेको फूललाई चुडेर गयौ,
तिम्रो हाँसोमा परेको पिरतीलाई नहेरी गयौ,
मन मरिसक्यो मुटु लिएर के गरूँ भन आफैँ, 
तिम्रो पासोमा परेको सिकारलाई नमारी गयौ।

title: काल प्रतीक्षा
summary: A ghazal written during a difficult moment while my grandfather, my childhood hero, was recovering after being discharged from the ICU.
background: This ghazal was written when my grandfather was seriously ill after being discharged from the ICU at Mechi Provincial Hospital to Model Ward.
dedication: To my grandfather, my childhood hero.
content:
# काल प्रतीक्षा

अहिल्यै आइज, कि त नआइज,
भागी जा, कि त लगी जा।


चाँडै आइज, कि त बाँच्न दे,
छोडी जा, कि त लगी जा।


सुटुक्क आइज, कि त भनेर आइज,
टाढै बस्, कि त लगी जा।


हसाउँदै लैजा, कि त समय दे,
सत्य बोल्, कि त लगी जा।


अहिल्यै आइज, कि त नआइज,
भागी जा, कि त लगी जा।

title: मेरो देश
summary: A poem reflecting my emotions as a Nepalese citizen after MCC agreement got passed by the Nepalese parliament.
background: This is the first poem ever written by me. It was written during my school days when I was in grade 8.
content:
# मेरो देश 

मेरो देश हो ईश्वरको मनोहर वर,
चार जात छत्तिस वर्णको प्यारो घर।
पवित्र छन यहाँका खोला र नदी,
जीवन दिन्छन् यिनले बस्दछन मेरो देशमा जति।


हेर्दा देखिएला मेरो देश सानो,
छैन यहाँ कसैको मन अरूप्रति बिरानो।
एक छ हिमाल, एक छ पहाड, एक छ तराई,
तर छैन यहाँ कोही पनि पराई।


नेपालीसँग तुलना गरिन्छन् चाँदी र सुन,
अङ्कित छन् यहाँ ध्वज तथा मनमा सूर्य र जून।
एक अर्काको दुख बोक्दछन् सबै भरिया सरी,
मेरो देशको गौरव गान गाउँदा अभिमान छाउँछ छाती भरी।


सीता, जनक तथा भृकुटीको हो थलो मेरो देश,
विश्वकै प्राचीन सभ्यता हो मेरो देश।
धर्तीकै अपार नमुना हो मेरो देश,
हरेक नेपालीको प्राण र अभिमान हो मेरो देश।


भाग्यशाली छ ऊ जसले यो देशमा जन्म लियो,
तर कोही अगि छैनन् आज मठ र गुम्बामा बाल्न दियो।
ईश्वर रचित मेरो देश आज किन पिछडियो,
व्यक्तिगत लाभको लागि किन
मेरो देशको कलेजो नै निचारियो।

title: तिमी गएपछि
summary: You got it well. Needs no explanation.
background: Just having fun with words and rhymes. This poem was written during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
content:
# तिमी गएपछि

बेकार मन खोलेजस्तो भयो तिमी गएपछि
आफ्नै आँखा पनि पराई लाग्यो तिमी गएपछि ।

जति मन फुकाएको थिएँ त्यति नै लाज भयो
शब्दहरूले पनि मलाई छोडे तिमी गएपछि ।

मनको कुरा पोख्नु कमजोरी हो भन्थे सबैले
मनका चोटले पनि यही पाठ पढाउँछन् तिमी गएपछि ।

सम्बन्ध टुटेको पीडा त सहन सकिन्थ्यो तर
लाजले बाँच्नै गाह्रो बनायो तिमी गएपछि ।

सम्बन्धहरूदेखि डर लाग्न थालेको छ अचेल
"किन?", ऐनाले समेत प्रश्न गर्‍यो तिमी गएपछि ।

मेरा आफन्त जब मेरो हालखबर सोध्छन्
करले मुस्कुराउँदै झुट बोल्नुपर्छ तिमी गएपछि ।

कयौँ प्रयत्न गर्दागर्दै पनि प्रीति जोगाउन सकिनँ
स्वार्थी छ जस्तो लाग्यो सारा संसार नै तिमी गएपछि ।

title: म फकत बसेँ।
background: This is the first gazal ever written by me for SWSC-organised Peepal Chautari Gazal Saanjh. It was written during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
content:
# म फकत बसेँ।

तिम्रै सुनील उज्यालो मुटुभरि बोकेर बसेँ,
तिमी आकाश भयौ म धर्ती भएर बसेँ।

जब तिमी दुई थोपा वर्षा बनी आएकी थियौ,
म आजीवन तिनै पल... पलपल सम्झेर बसेँ।

तिमीलाई छुने रहरमा कैयौँ पर्वत उठाएँ,
हरेक चोटलाई आफ्नै भाग्य सम्झेर बसेँ।

तिमी वर्षा बनी आयौ र चुपचाप फर्कियौ फेरि,
म झ्यालबाट एक्लै तिम्रो बाटो हेरेर बसेँ।

तिमी निठुरी बतास भयौ उडी गयौ टाढा कतै,
म भने बादलको आगमन पर्खेर बसेँ।

तिमी हिउँ बनी झर्यौ मेरा उजाड पर्वतहरूमाथि,
पीडामा म पत्थरझैँ पग्लिन नसकी अडिएर बसेँ।

धर्ती र आकाशको दूरी कहिल्यै मेटिएन आखिर,
म क्षितिजले देखाउने झूटो सपना केलाएर बसेँ।

तिमी टाढा दुलही बन्यौ जीवनको अर्कै मोडमा,
म  अँध्यारा रातहरूमा उज्यालो पर्खेर बसेँ।

'प्रशम' समयले सबै घाउ निको पार्छ भन्छन्,
(तर खै...) 
म खरानी भइसकेपछि पनि बलर, जलेर, डढेर बसेँ।

title: बालबालिकाका लागि वित्तीय शिक्षा
summary: Financial education is a must for every student in economically volatile nations like Nepal.
background: Addressing the emptiness and voidness of financial literacy in school-level education in Nepal. This article was written during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
content:
# बालबालिकाका लागि वित्तीय शिक्षा

हामीले “सानैदेखि पैसा जोगाउनु पर्छ, अनावश्यक खर्च गर्नु हुँदैन र पैसा रूखमा फल्दैन ।” भनेर सुनिआएका छौँ । तर पैसाले कसरी काम गर्छ भन्ने कुरा थाहा नपाई नै बालकहरू युवावस्थामा पुग्छन्।

कक्षा १२ उत्तीर्ण गरिसकेका, गणितका जटिलभन्दा जटिल समस्या र समिकरणहरू हल गर्न सक्ने विद्यार्थीलाई बजेट, निक्षेप, ऋणपत्र, धितोपत्र, ब्याजदर, आर्थिक नीति, मुद्रास्फिति, मुद्रसंकुचन, पुँजी, कर प्रणाली, इत्यादि कुराहरू भनेकै थाहा हुँदैन ।

आखिर वित्तीय साक्षरता किन नेपालमा कम छ होला ?

वित्तीय साक्षरता भनेको आर्थिक र वित्तीय (पैसासँग सम्बन्धीत) यस्तो क्षमता हो जसले एउटा मानिसलाई कमाएको वा उपलब्ध पैसालाई उचित रूपमा जोगाउन, सापटी लिन/दिन, लगानी गर्न र बाँडफाँड गर्न सक्ने बनाउँछ । त्यसो भन्दै गर्दा, यो पैसा व्यवस्थापन गर्न मात्र चाहिने चिज भने होइन । यसले हामीलाई उचित आर्थिक निर्णय लिन र दीर्घकालीन आर्थिक समृद्धिको मार्गतर्फ बढाउँछ ।

नेपाल जस्तो आर्थिक रूपमा अस्थिर अर्थतन्त्रदेश, जहाँ डिजिटल भुक्तानी, अनलाइन बैंकिङ र अनौपचारिक रोजगारीको दर बढ्दो छ; वित्तीय साक्षरता अब कदापि वैकल्पिक विषय होइन । हाम्रा मागहरूका लागि यो अनिवार्य भइसकेको छ ।

जो विद्यार्थीले खल्ती खर्च व्यवस्थापन गर्न सक्छ, व्यक्तिगत खर्चहरूको अनुगमन गर्न सक्छ, अनि सौख र आवश्यकताबीचको भिन्नता समयमै बुझ्छ – ऊ पछि गएर पक्कै पनि पैसाको मामिलामा अनुशासित व्यक्ति बन्छ‌ । यद्यपि, मैले भने जेन–जी र जेन–अल्फा उमेरवर्गका बालबालिकाहरूमा पैसा जोगाउने बानी एकदमै कम देखेको छु ।

युवा अवस्थामा पुगिसकेपछि, वास्तविक जीवनमा आइपर्ने आर्थिक चुनौतीहरू सामना गर्न सक्ने क्षमता तपाईंका छोराछोरीहरूमा छ त ?

वित्तीय साक्षरता नभएकाहरूका लागि स-साना आर्थिक चुनौती पनि ठूलो महसूस हुन सक्छ । बजेटिङ, कर र बैंकिङ प्रणाल, बीमा, बजार, पूँजी परिचालन, ऋण व्यवस्थापन, खाक नियन्त्रण इत्यादि विषयहरूको आधारभूत ज्ञान मात्र भएको खण्डमा त्यस्ता चुनौतीहरू पार गर्न ठूलो मद्दत पुग्न सक्छ ।

मोबाइल बैंकिङ र डिजिटल वालेट (Esewa, Khalti, Fonepay) जस्ता सेवाहरूले हाम्रो जीवन सहज बनाएकै हो । अब आफ्नो बैंक खाताबाट पैसा झिक्न एटिएम धाइराख्नु पर्दैन । तर यसका आफ्नै जोखिमहरू पनि छन् । एटिएमबाट तपाईंले निश्चित पैसा मात्र झिक्नुहुन्थ्यो । अब मोबाइल बैंकङ र डिजिटल वालेट तपाईंसँग हुनुको मतलब हो – तपाईंको जिन्दगी भरिको बचत/निक्षेप अब तपाईंको औँलाकैे टुप्पोमा छ । डिजिटल घोटाला, ठगी, र बैमानीहरू त छँदैछन् नै । यी सेवाहरूको सावधानीपूर्वक सदुपयोग गर्न वित्तीय साक्षरताले हामीलाई यहाँ पनि सहयोग गर्छ किनभने डिजिटल अर्थतन्त्रमा यी सेवाहरू चाहिन्छन् पनि ।

त्यति मात्रै नभएर, यसले हामीलाई पैसा/वित्तलाई हेर्ने नयाँ कोण दिन्छ । वित्त र पूँजी परिचालन गर्दा आत्मविश्वास दिन्छ । नयाँ व्यवसाय, अविष्कार र समग्र आर्थिक उन्नतिको मार्ग प्रदर्शन गर्दछ ।

यति हुँदाहुँदै पनि, पाठ्यक्रम र विद्यालयहरूमा वित्तीय शिक्षाको घनत्व निकै कम देखिन्छ । सैद्धान्तिक ज्ञानले मात्र पुग्दैन, शिक्षा त यथार्थ जीवनमा उपयोगी पनि हुनुपर्छ । ऐच्छिक प्रथम विषयहरूको श्रेणीमा अर्थशास्त्र विषय त छ तर यो विषयको पढाई केही मात्र विद्यालयहरूमा हुन्छ । मैले चिनेको एकजना हाल कक्षा –१२ मा व्यवस्थापन संकायमा अध्ययनरत छात्रा भन्छिन्, “अर्थशास्त्र विषय जहाँ पढाई हुन्छ, त्यहाँ पनि विद्यार्थीहरूले पाठ्यक्रम र वास्तविक जीवनका विषयहरूमा ठूलो अन्तर महसूस गर्छन् । पाठ्यक्रमको कुरा जीवनसँग मेल नखाए जस्तो हुँदा दिमागमा घुस्दैन र पढ्ने, सिक्ने, जान्ने, इच्छा पनि मर्दै जान्छ ।”

परिणामस्वरूप विद्यार्थीहरू ए प्लस र ए ग्रेडको नतिजा ल्याएर उत्तीर्ण त हुन्छन्, तर आफ्नै व्यक्तिगत वित्त (Personal Finance) लाई सुदृढ गराउने सीप र ज्ञान उनीहरूसँग हुँदैन ।

वित्तीय साक्षरता प्रवर्धन गर्न अर्को छुट्टै विषय ल्याउनु पर्छ भन्ने पनि छैन, अनिवार्य र अन्य ऐच्छिक विषयहरूमा यसका मूल कुराहरू समावेश गर्दा पनि ठूलो प्रभाव पर्न सक्छ । तर फेरि जानकारी र ज्ञान मात्र दिने शिक्षा पनि काम छैन, त्यसरी हामी हालकै भन्ने कि परम्परागत, त्यही तरिकामा पुनः जान्छौं । विद्यार्थीहरूले उक्त शिक्षाबाट आफ्नो व्यवहारमा पनि परिवर्तन ल्याउन सक्नुपर्छ ।

निष्कर्षमा, वित्तीय साक्षरता भनेको एउटा शैक्षिक विषय मात्र नभएर वास्तविक जीवनमा अत्यावश्यक सीप हो । यसले प्रत्यक्ष रूपमा आत्मनिर्भरता, स्थिरता र भावी समृद्धिलाई सुनिश्चित गर्न ठूलो टेवा पुर्याउँछ । पढाइको रणभूमिमा विजयी भएर, बिना तयारी सिधै कमाईको रणभूमिमा जाने विद्यार्थीहरूको सङ्ख्या नेपालमा ठूलो छ । आत्मविश्वास, साहस र स्पष्ट आर्थिक लक्ष्य देख्ने र देख्न सक्ने खालका विद्यार्थीहरू शून्यभन्दा केही मात्रै धेर छन् । त्यसैले वित्तीय साक्षरतालाई प्रवर्धन गर्न वित्तीय शिक्षा वर्तमान युवापिढीको आवश्यकता हो । यो सन्देश सबै सम्बन्धित निकायसम्म पुगोस् ।

title: The Crisis of Leadership in the Age of Viral Fame
summary: Viral fame may shape today's headlines, but history ultimately remembers those who choose service over popularity and principle over applause.
background: Trying to question the impact of viral fame on leadership. This article was written during my post +2 board exam leisure time.
dedication: To all the netizens and the public.
content:
# The Crisis of Leadership in the Age of Viral Fame

Commanding public attention has become easier than ever. You only need a smartphone, a compelling video, and an algorithm. These combined can transform an unknown individual into a global sensation overnight. Yet, while influence has become highly accessible, genuine leadership seems increasingly scarce in the contemporary society. In this digital era, popularity is often mistaken for credibility. Visibility for significance and virality for leadership. This confusion has created one of the most visible challenges of our time.

History remembers individuals not because they attracted attention. They accepted responsibility in order to be remembered. Most of the political reformers, social activists, and visionary entrepreneurs who shaped history did so by making difficult decisions. It would be typically at the cost of their own popularity. Leadership has always been measured by impact rather than applause.

Social media has indeed made communication democratic. It has enabled ordinary people to share ideas and educate millions in ways that were unimaginable just two decades ago. We have seen many creators use these platforms to improve lives, raise awareness, and inspire meaningful actions. Social media itself is not the problem. It is the culture that increasingly equates attention to authority. In a country where social media increasingly influences public disclosures, distinguishing popularity from leadership has become crucial.

It is a well-known fact that social media platforms do not necessarily reward wisdom. They reward content that generates engagement. Their algorithms are generally optimized to maximize engagement, including clicks, shares, comments, and watch time. This often amplifies content that provokes outrage, controversy, or strong emotion. Thus, visibility is frequently driven by the ability to capture attention rather than expertise or integrity. The loudest voices often tend to dominate the thoughtful ones.

Let us consider two pieces of content published on the same day: a meaningful lecture explaining inflation and a sensational prank video designed to provoke reactions. Which one is more likely to spread widely? You know the answer.

Likewise, a university professor may devote decades to research that shapes public policy, while a fifteen-second viral video reaches millions within hours. Visibility and contribution are no longer closely aligned today. Digital platforms are not inherently biased against expertise. Nevertheless, they are simply designed to reward what keeps users engaged. The result is that entertainment often travels farther than thoughtful analysis.

This environment blurs the difference between influencers and leaders. Influencers might excel at attracting audiences. Leaders accept responsibility for those they serve. Influencers may shape trends and opinions. But leaders shape institutions, organizations, communities, and nations. One measures success through engagement metrics. The other through trust, accountability, and lasting change. The two roles, however, are not mutually exclusive, but they are fundamentally different.

In recent years, digital culture has increasingly rewarded those who respond to what is immediately popular rather than what is ultimately right. Political leaders, institutions, and public figures regularly face immense pressure to make decisions based on online trends and public outrage instead of long-term principles. When popularity becomes the primary objective, difficult yet necessary decisions are frequently postponed indefinitely, accountability weakens, and ultimately leadership becomes mere performance.

This distinction matters because leadership often requires the courage to disappoint people. A responsible leader must sometimes make decisions that invite criticism in the present to secure stability or progress in the future. History repeatedly shows that transformative leadership rarely enjoys universal approval at the moment it is exercised. Abraham Lincoln faced fierce opposition during the American Civil War. Nelson Mandela endured decades of imprisonment before becoming a symbol of reconciliation. Hence, legacies are built not on immediate popularity but on unwavering commitment to justice, truth, and principle.

Trust, not attention, is the true currency of leadership. Attention can be purchased through advertising, manufactured through controversy, or accumulated through algorithms. Trust, however, is earned gradually through consistency, competence, and accountability. While a viral moment may attract millions of viewers, only sustained character earns lasting respect.

None of this suggests that influencers cannot become leaders. Many content creators have successfully mobilized charitable initiatives, promoted education, and advocated for important social causes. Likewise, holding a formal position of authority does not automatically make someone a leader. Leadership is defined neither by profession nor by platform but by the willingness to accept responsibility for others and to prioritize long-term public good over personal recognition. The issue is not that some people become famous; the issue is when fame itself becomes mistaken for evidence of wisdom, competence, or character.

The greater challenge for modern society is therefore not the abundance of influencers but the scarcity of discernment. Citizens must learn to differentiate between those who merely command attention and those who genuinely deserve trust. In an era where every voice can be amplified, the ability to identify principled and accountable leadership becomes an essential civic responsibility.

When societies mistake popularity for leadership, they risk elevating those who command attention over those capable of solving complex problems. Although technology will continue to evolve and digital influence will become even more powerful, the qualities that define leadership remain remarkably unchanged: integrity, courage, responsibility, and vision.

Viral fame may shape today's headlines, but history ultimately remembers those who choose service over popularity and principle over applause.

title: तिम्रो चाहना छैन मलाई
content:
# तिम्रो चाहना छैन मलाई

आज साँझ तिमीलाई देखे,
फेरि प्रेमिपनमा पो पुगेछु,
तिमीलाई देखेर कता चिसो बतास चले जस्तो भयो,
मेरो जीउ कामेको होकी भनेको त,
मन तरङ्गित भएको थाहा भयो।

खोई काहाँबाट आउँछन् यस्ता तरङ्गहरु कुन्नि,
पागल त पक्कै छुइन म पनि,
तर खोई तिमीलाई हेर्दाहेर्दै थुप्रै बेर टोलाएछु,
तिम्रो प्रतीक्षा त गरेको थिइन मैले,
तर तिमीलाई बाटोमा देख्दा यसै रमाएछु।

तिमीलाई देखेको आदि घण्टा बितिसकेछ,
तिम्रै मात्र सम्झनामा पो अल्झिएछु क्यारे,
कुन गीत कुन ताल भन्नु खोई यो तरङ्गीले,
प्रेम अन्धो हुन्छ अरे,
मलाई त बहिरो पनि पो बनाएछ यसले।

माया मारेको छैन बस्,
संसारमा तिमीलाई सबैभन्दा बढी माया गर्ने म नै हो।
तिम्रो कुनै चाहना छैन मलाई हेर,
तिमीलाई खुशी देख्ने रहर मात्र हो।
